articles.title: One still missing after Grand Canyon floods kill two and prompt rescue efforts
articles.summary: Almost everyone is now accounted for after dozens of hikers were airlifted to safety, an official says.
articles.body:
All but one person missing after flash flooding devastated parts of the Grand Canyon has now been found, the National Parks Service (NPS) says.

Thirty people had previously been unaccounted for, but rangers "worked tirelessly" to reduce that number, Incident Commander Dave Black told reporters on Monday.

At least two people died after floodwaters struck on Saturday afternoon, wiping out footbridges and propelling boulders downstream.

Crews had "worked incredibly hard trying to get this situation under control", Black said during Monday's press conference.

This involved the airlift of dozens of people in Phantom Ranch, one of the park's hardest-hit areas, he added.

An initial 45 people were evacuated by air on Saturday, and a remaining group of 37 were later evacuated by Sunday afternoon, Black said.

"We've had a very busy couple of days," the official added.

Crews will be deployed on Tuesday morning to search for the final missing person in the area between Phantom Ranch and Cottonwood Manzanita.

Further heavy rain was forecast overnight from Monday into Tuesday, bringing an elevated risk of additional flash flooding to the area.

Black described the two individuals who died as adult males, adding he would not disclose any further details about their identities.

The NPS earlier said it had found the body of a 46-year-old man near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River.

The "significant" flooding began in Bright Angel Canyon around 14:30 local time (19:30 BST) on Saturday, the NPS previously said.

Nikki Baggs, 41, who was among those to be airlifted out of the bottom of the Grand Canyon with her two friends, told the BBC: "The whole thing was terrifying.

"It was a beautiful day and then people were screaming, running."

Nearly all footbridges across Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, and the parks service closed down Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground, the entire North Kaibab Trail to Phantom Ranch, Black Bridge, Silver Bridge and the Colorado River.

On Monday, the NPS said that preliminary assessments indicated about 40% of the Transcanyon Waterline, which delivers water for visitors and approximately 2,500 residents, was damaged or destroyed in the flood.

The Grand Canyon is one of the most popular national parks in the US, with about five million people visiting each year. The Bright Angel trail is its most popular hike.

The recent rains in the Grand Canyon area, and more widely in south-western parts of the US, are due to monsoonal showers.

A change in wind direction at this time of year pulls warm, moist air northward from the Gulf of California and the tropical Pacific, triggering storms over mountainous terrain.

The storms are difficult to pinpoint in forecasts and so can strike without warning. But because the ground is usually very dry, any heavy downpours lead to dangerous flash flooding and frequent lightning which increases the threat of wildfires.

articles.title: The Rs 2.05 crore question: Can Meta be blamed for what its glasses record?
articles.summary: India News: A Delhi man has sent a legal notice to an Instagram creator and Meta Platforms after he was allegedly harassed and covertly filmed at a café using Ray.
articles.body: A Delhi man has sent a legal notice to an Instagram creator and Meta Platforms after he was allegedly harassed and covertly filmed at a café using Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.The footage was subsequently posted on Instagram and viewed more than 4.19 lakh times.He has demanded that the video be removed, an apology issued and ₹2.05 crore paid in damages.But the notice, issued on August 24, goes beyond the actions of the creator. It seeks to hold Meta responsible in two capacities: as the owner of Instagram, which allegedly continued to host the reel after receiving complaints, and as the technology company behind the design and marketing of the camera-equipped glasses used to record it.The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), which provided the victim pro bono legal assistance, says this is, to its knowledge, among the first legal actions in India to directly raise the liability of a smart-glasses maker for harm allegedly enabled by its product design.The case has not been decided by a court yet and the claims in the notice, so far, remain allegations. The man, whose identity has been withheld and who is referred to as X, is represented by advocate Apar Gupta.So, what allegedly happened?According to IFF, X was sitting alone at a Costa Coffee outlet in Delhi’s Khan Market on July 24 when a stranger, who eventually turned out to be a creator, approached him.The creator allegedly pestered and insulted him with unsolicited questions and remarks and followed him inside the café. X complained to the staff and eventually moved to another seating area to get away from the unpleasant situation thrust upon him.What he did not know, IFF says, was that the encounter was allegedly being recorded through Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. One or more of the creator’s associates also allegedly filmed the exchange from other angles without his knowledge or consent.The footage was posted as an Instagram reel on July 26. By August 6, according to IFF, it had received more than 4.19 lakh views, approximately 15,700 likes and over 500 comments.X reported both the video and the account to Instagram on July 27. According to IFF, the reporting menu offered no category specifically covering invasion of privacy or non-consensual recording. The victim, therefore, selected “bullying or harassment”.He also submitted a separate complaint to Meta’s grievance officer for India under “Privacy violation — sharing of personal information or representation without consent.”Instagram subsequently informed him that the reported material doesn’t go against its “Community Standards”, according to IFF.Why has Meta been named?The most significant part of the notice concerns the glasses themselves.Developed by Meta in partnership with eyewear company EssilorLuxottica, Ray-Ban Meta glasses resemble conventional eyewear but allow users to take photographs and record videos hands-free. They were launched in India in May 2025 at a starting price of ₹29,900.The glasses have a small white capture LED on the front that indicates when the camera is being used. The notice argues that this warning is inadequate because it can easily be missed by someone who does not know that the glasses contain a camera.“The recording indicator on the said devices is inadequate and easily overlooked, and the harm that eventuated to our client is due to a design that is foreseeably enabled,” the notice states.It argues that Meta “owed and breached a duty of care” to X and was negligent in contributing to the alleged intrusion into his privacy.Crucially, the notice argues that this liability arises from Meta’s own product-design and marketing decisions and is therefore separate from its role as an online intermediary.Section 79 of the Information Technology Act provides conditional protection to online intermediaries against liability for content posted by third parties. The notice contends that such protection cannot extend to a negligence claim arising from Meta’s own product design.That argument has not yet been tested in court.The Delhi dispute could now test a different question: whether a company that makes wearable cameras has a responsibility not merely to indicate that recording is taking place, but to ensure that an unsuspecting bystander can reasonably understand that they are being filmed.To know more, subscribe and read the full story on TOI+ —Secretly filmed by Meta glasses: Why a Delhi man is demanding Rs 2.05 croreWhat Meta says about safeguards against covert recordingWhat studies have found about privacy and camera-equipped glassesWhat the legal notice demands from Meta and the Instagram creatorGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘It wasn't the lake’: Why global warming and poor monitoring may have led to Nepal floods
articles.summary: South Asia News: The catastrophic Nepal tragedy has now claimed more than a thousand lives while several still remain missing as rescue teams continue working to reach.
articles.body: The catastrophic Nepal tragedy has now claimed more than a thousand lives while several still remain missing as rescue teams continue working to reach communities cut off by destroyed roads, bridges and landslides.Nepal's disaster agency said on Tuesday that 3,916 people remain missing, including 583 foreigners, while at least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, with emergency crews using helicopters and other aircraft to reach stranded communities where floodwaters and landslides have severed road links.Initial reports hinted at the collapse of a “dam” or barrier, leading to the catastrophe. However, the flood that tore through Nepal's Rasuwa district and across the border into Tibet on 26 August did not begin with a “barrier lake” bursting its banks.Barrier lakeA barrier lake, in scientific terms, forms when landslide debris, ice or sediment suddenly blocks a river and holds water behind what is, in effect, an accidental dam. As experts consulted by the UK's Science Media Centre put it, unlike an engineered reservoir, such a dam's "geometry, internal structure and stability are therefore highly uncertain." These features are notoriously unstable and short-lived.In the case of Nepal, once the initial flood had passed, debris left behind by the avalanche blocked river channels and allowed water to pool.However, the barrier lakes that formed downstream evolved rapidly and unpredictably in the days that followed. China's ministry of water resources measured the main dam on August 27 at roughly 150 metres long and 40 to 50 metres deep, holding between 1.5 and 2 million cubic metres of water, and warned that a further 3 million cubic metres, described as equivalent to around 1,200 Olympic swimming pools, could flow in over the following three days.By August 28 the lake had overflowed, forcing Nepal to halt helicopter rescue operations for 90 minutes as residents in Rasuwa ran to higher ground, Reuters reported. Satellite imagery on August 29 showed the lake shrinking to around 99,000 square metres, roughly the size of 14 football pitches, before China's water ministry reported on August 30 that it had essentially drained through a natural channel.A second, larger body of water was also spotted by satellite immediately below the glacier-collapse scar, and unlike the first lake, it initially had no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could keep building behind it. Chinese officials described the feature as an "impact crater" formed by the glacier fall. Chen Hongqi, a senior engineer at China's Geological Disaster Technical Guidance Center, said at the time: "We estimate its area to be over 120,000 square metres, but its depth is currently unknown."Barrier lakes of this kind are inherently short-lived. A review of 1,267 documented landslide dam failures cited in the Science Media Centre's briefing on the disaster found that 91.8 per cent fail simply by overtopping their banks, with no engineered spillway to control the release. Of those failures, 87 per cent occurred within a year of the dam forming, 71 per cent within a month, and 51 per cent within a single day.The lakes were a threat, not the causeSpeaking to TOI, Dr Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, head of the Department of Environmental Science at Kathmandu University, said the disaster's origin lay entirely in the glacier itself."The initial event on the 26, there was no involvement of lakes," Kayastha said. "Only glacier ice collapsed from high altitude. It was around 5,200 metres. A huge amount of ice fell, and it took another ice mass lying on the lower part of the same glacier, he said.“Those two ice masses rushed down, converted to water and debris. We had a deadly flood downstream."The ice-rock avalanche moved with extraordinary speed, covering around 22 kilometres to Rasuwagadhi in just over seven minutes, according to a preliminary study by Nepalese scientists.The mass travelled at an estimated average speed of 46.3 metres per second, or about 167 kmph, as it plunged from the high Himalayas into the river system below, news agency PTI reported.That single event set off a chain of destruction that has claimed almost a thousand lives, with a potential rise in numbers.There was another misconception that the floods were caused by an earthquake. The US Geological Survey had recorded a tremor of magnitude 5.2, not from an earthquake, but from the seismic energy generated by the collapsing ice mass itself. Water levels on the Trishuli River rose by as much as nine metres in 30 minutes at Galchhi and seven metres over a similar period at Malekhu.Nepal's ministry of energy, water resources and irrigation later assessed damage to 27 power projects totalling 901.1 megawatts of capacity, including a fully destroyed substation, along with dozens of bridges and an 80km stretch of road to the Chinese border."A part of the lower part of the glacier fell down from 5,200 metres to 3,800 metres, so the vertical height was 1,400 metres," Kayastha said, describing the scale of the collapse. This is the professor's characterisation of the trigger; it is his explanation of the physical mechanism, based on his reading of what occurred, rather than a claim he presents as beyond dispute.According to Kayastha, the barrier lakes that dominated the days of coverage that followed were a secondary phenomenon.What led to the glacial collapse?Kayastha links the instability of the glacier itself to warming temperatures."We can blame global warming, because nowadays temperature is increasing, and when we have higher temperature, more ice will melt at those altitudes also," he said.Meltwater, he explained, finds its way into cracks in the glacier. "That meltwater goes and penetrates down, and there are a lot of crevices on that glacier. If we check the previous satellite images, we can see many cracks, meaning crevices." Once inside those cracks, he said, the water works its way toward the base of the glacier: "When it reaches the bedrock, because at the bottom we have a rock, that cracked portion from the crack portion can slide. That was what happened on the 26th event."This is not, in Kayastha's account, an isolated incident. "Last year also we had the same glacial flood on July 8, 2025, and before that we had one glacial lake flood in the Khumbu region near Namche, which happened on August 16, 2024," he said. "All three were during the monsoon period. That is mainly due to the increase in temperature. In one or two weeks, if the temperature increases quite high, movement will occur, and such things may happen."In fact, months before the devastating floods, two landmark reports by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) had warned that rapidly melting glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya(HKH) were escalating the risks of catastrophic floods and other cryosphere-related disasters. Released in March 2026, the reports found that glacier ice loss across the region had doubled since 2000, with the smallest and most vulnerable glaciers shrinking rapidly and intensifying hazards such as glacial lakeNotably, Nepal was ranked the sixth most affected country in the world for 2024 by Germanwatch's Climate Risk Index 2026, a measure of recorded deaths, people affected and economic losses from extreme weather that year.Meltwater, monsoon and monitoringKayastha believes such events, though difficult to catch, are not beyond prediction. "It's not impossible, it's possible. But we have to monitor, we have to visualise many, many satellites continuously," he said, noting that crevices widen visibly before a collapse.He set out what an early-warning system should look like, i.e. satellite monitoring of glacier movement, combined with water-level sensors installed at two points downstream, "one upper site, one lower site", so that a sudden rise can be flagged before a flood arrives. For remote terrain like the Langtang region, he suggested field cameras capable of monitoring from several kilometres away, watched around the clock.The obstacles, in his view, are not technical. "The only problem here in Nepal's society is that one is the finance, the other one is, I think, the willingness or promptness, how seriously the political people take such issues," he said."We don't have any technical and manpower or human resource issues."He also pointed to the practical risks people face during the monsoon, when rivers can be blocked upstream without warning."If the river stops for a few minutes or a few hours, then they should be very careful about what happened upstream," he said, adding that people should identify evacuation routes in advance. He expects consequences for Nepal's tourism-dependent economy."There is a high chance of impact on Nepal's economy, and yes, there will be fewer tourists," he said, calling for clearer guidance on when travel in the Himalayas is safe. "Please avoid travelling during the monsoon period in the Himalayas mainly," he said.The Nepal tragedy is a reminder that in a warming Himalayas, disasters can unfold faster than warnings can reach people. For Nepal, the challenge now is to turn lessons from the catastrophe into better monitoring and quicker evacuation before the next glacier gives way.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Fears branch cutting could damage stressed trees in Jersey
articles.summary: The annual branchage is dictated by a law from 1915and scheduled for Friday.
articles.body:
A farmer working to regenerate soil at a former potato farm has said an enforced date for cutting branches would cause unnecessary damage to trees after a "brutal summer" of drought.

The deadline for the annual branchage - a legal requirement designed to keep roads safe - is set by parish constables and this year falls on Friday.

Organic farmer Nikki de Gruchy criticised being "forced" to cut "already stressed" 30-year-old bows on an "arbitrary date" when it could be delayed to adhere to "conditions on the ground".

Andy Jehan, chairman of the constables committee, said it had been an "unusual summer", they would be happy to "speak to the industry about future years".

He added the 1914 law which dictates the date-setting was "being reviewed".

De Gruchy said she had written to leaders to voice her concerns and urge them to consider branchage dates based on "prevailing conditions on the ground" as opposed to a date "set a year in advance".

The farmer, who in 2023 used an ancient legal injunction to prevent branchage by a road she claimed went through her land, said trees had responded to the heatwave conditions by starting to shed their leaves early, while the bows had "dropped a lot".

She said when trees like the chestnut had shed their nuts she expected these bows to lift in time - removing the need for the same level of cutting.

"If we delay then we don't have to cut as many trees," she added.

She said there needed to be an "update in thinking".

Andy Howell, constable of Trinity, said conditions had been "tough" for farmers, plants and animals.

She said the dates for the branchage were set a year in advance, and the work had to be completed by law.

She said advance planning meant volunteer parishioners who carried out the work could "plan their diaries in advance".

She added: "The parish is extremely grateful to our honorary police and to all our volunteers who give up their valuable time to help our community."

She said the branchage in Trinity would take place on 4 September and noted "other landowners" in the parish had "already completed their branchages".

articles.title: Government updates on new laws to tackle rogue funeral firms
articles.summary: The government plans to regulate undertakers after the jailing of Hull funeral director Robert Bush.
articles.body:
A minister has said the government is working on new laws to "drive rogue operators out of the funeral industry".

Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Yvette Cooper gave a written update to Parliament on proposed legislation to regulate undertakers.

It comes after a Hull funeral home director was jailed last month for failing to bury or cremate people and giving bereaved relatives the ashes of strangers.

Robert Bush was sent to prison for 20 years after he admitted 67 offences, including denying 30 people a decent and proper burial, theft from charities, and fraudulent trading over a period of almost 12 years.

During his sentencing, Hull Crown Court heard that 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes were found by police raiding Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in March 2024.

Bush, 48, of Otley in West Yorkshire, was "preoccupied with his own enrichment", defrauded nearly 200 families out of £562,117 and "caused anguish and pain on a scale beyond comprehension", the judge said.

Cooper said Bush's actions were "utterly abhorrent, and my thoughts remain with all the bereaved families in Hull who were so badly let down."

She said that, as part of the plans, the Law Commission would review the criminal law in relation to the deceased and "consider any gaps in existing legal protections and make recommendations on the creation of new offences, if they are needed".

Cooper said detailed plans and the timetable for their introduction would be announced "in due course".

The funeral industry in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is currently self-regulating, relying on voluntary codes and inspections by trade associations.

Anyone can set up as a funeral director without formal training, registration or oversight.

MPs and families affected by Bush's crimes have been lobbying for change.

Nigel Hotham's uncle, Mark Hotham, died in September 2023 and his body was later found in Bush's funeral parlour.

"It's easier to open a funeral director's than it is to open a sandwich shop – and there's more regulation around sandwich shops than there is funeral directors," he said.

articles.title: This Nebraska town once had 150 residents, shops and a school. Today, one 84-year-old woman serves as mayor and runs it alone
articles.summary: US News: Five miles from the South Dakota border, a dirt road winds through the Nebraska prairie towards a town that has almost vanished. Monowi still has its .
articles.body: Five miles from the South Dakota border, a dirt road winds through the Nebraska prairie towards a town that has almost vanished. Monowi still has its street signs, a few battered buildings and three lampposts, but there is only one person left to see them each morning. Elsie Eiler, 84, lives in a trailer beside the town’s small tavern, which she opens for customers who travel from miles away. She pours the drinks, cooks the food and keeps the books. She is also Monowi’s mayor, clerk, treasurer and librarian.In a place where the old church stands empty and weeds have begun to swallow the remains of houses, Eiler’s routine has become an unusual thread connecting the town’s past with its present. Once home to about 150 people during its railway-era heyday, Monowi now depends on one resident to keep its name, lights and doors alive.How a Nebraska farm girl became Monowi’s final residentEiler’s unusual position came about gradually rather than through some sudden disappearance. Monowi had once been a small but active railway community. During the 1930s, around 150 people lived there, with shops, restaurants, a school and even a prison. The railway brought movement through the town, while farming supported the families who lived nearby.Eiler grew up close by, on a farm only a short walk from Monowi. Her connection to the place went back to childhood. She met Rudy, the man she would eventually marry, at the local one-room schoolhouse. They later travelled by bus to secondary school seven miles away, before their lives briefly took them in different directions.According to the BBC, Rudy joined the US Air Force and served in France during the Korean War. Eiler went to Kansas City, where she found work with an airline and hoped eventually to become a stewardess. The city did not suit her. Monowi was home, and she returned.She and Rudy married when she was 19 and raised two children. Their connection with the tavern became another part of that long attachment to the town. Rudy suggested restoring an old bar that had once belonged to Eiler’s father. They reopened it in 1971.The last neighbours disappeared, leaving Eiler to carry on aloneThe changes were not unique to Monowi. Across the Great Plains, rural communities struggled as farming conditions deteriorated and local economies weakened after the Second World War. Families left, businesses closed and the services that once held small settlements together gradually vanished. Monowi followed that pattern piece by piece.BBC reported, Eiler’s father’s funeral in 1960 was the last held in the town’s wooden church. The post office disappeared later in the decade, followed by the remaining grocery shops. The school closed in 1974. By the middle of the 1970s, Eiler’s own children had left to find work elsewhere.By 1980, only 18 people remained. Two decades later, just Eiler and Rudy were still living there. They continued working at the tavern together, even as the surrounding buildings emptied. When Rudy died in 2004, the population fell from two to one.That left Eiler with an extraordinary collection of civic responsibilities.The woman who serves as mayor, clerk and tavern ownerMonowi is an incorporated place, meaning Eiler is not simply the last person living in an abandoned settlement. She remains responsible for the machinery of local government. Each year, she puts up a notice for the mayoral election at the tavern. Then she votes for herself.She also prepares the town’s municipal road plan so it can receive state funding. Around $500 in annual taxes comes from Eiler herself, helping pay for the town’s three street lamps and its water supply.The arrangement becomes even more unusual when alcohol and tobacco licences are involved. Applications arrive at the village secretary’s office. Eiler is the secretary. She signs the documents in her capacity as clerk, then receives the licences as the owner of the tavern. She even keeps an eye on the vacant residential lots, just in case somebody decides to move in and increase Monowi’s population from one to two.The last resident has built a life filled with familiar facesFor all the talk about Eiler living alone, the Monowi of her everyday life is not particularly empty.Her home is only a few steps from the tavern. At about nine each morning, except on Mondays when she takes the day off, she walks over and opens the doors. Many of the customers come from communities 20 or 30 miles away. Some travel much farther. People from Lincoln and Omaha, roughly 200 miles away, have also made the journey to visit her.The tavern has become the kind of place that rural pubs and cafés often are: somewhere people exchange local news, mark family occasions and run into people they have known for years.Graduation announcements, baptism invitations and Christmas cards are pinned to the bulletin board. Sunday evenings bring a game of Euchre, with players sometimes travelling for an hour to take part. Eiler cooks burgers, hot dogs and gizzards while customers sit around the bar and catch up. Eiler has watched children grow up and eventually arrive with children of their own. That history gives the tavern a role that goes well beyond serving food and beer.So when people ask whether she feels lonely, her answer is simple. People are always arriving and leaving.A 5,000-book library keeps Rudy’s memory aliveJust beside Eiler’s home and the tavern stands another reminder of the life Monowi once had. It is Rudy’s Library, a modest shed created from his personal collection. Rudy had been an enthusiastic reader, and before his death he wanted his books to become available to other people. He ordered a 320-square-foot building and packed his collection of around 5,000 books and magazines inside. He died before the project was finished.The family completed it afterwards. Eiler’s children wired the lights, nephews installed shelves and grandchildren painted the sign.Today, visitors can borrow books simply by taking the key from the tavern and using the library on an honour system. The shelves contain everything from Goethe to old issues of National Geographic.Monowi vanished from the map, but visitors kept comingAfter Rudy’s death, Monowi overtook nearby Gross, Nebraska, which had two residents, and became the only incorporated town in the United States with a population of one, according to the Census information cited in the source.Eiler keeps four guest books at the tavern, filled with signatures from people who have travelled from around the world. The attention was never something she had planned for. She simply happened to remain where she had always lived while the population around her dwindled away.The publicity brought attention to a part of Nebraska that might otherwise have remained largely unknown. There is also something slightly strange about the contrast. Monowi has almost disappeared as a residential community, yet the last person living there has made it a destination.The last resident had spent too much of her life here to simply leaveEiler has family elsewhere. She has two children, five grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. The nearest family member lives about 90 miles away in Ponca, Nebraska, while others live much farther away, including in Arizona and the Netherlands.But leaving Monowi would also mean leaving behind the friendships, routines and familiar places that have accumulated over a lifetime. She has spent decades in the same landscape. The tavern connects her with people she has known since they were young, and Rudy’s books remain within reach.For Eiler, the argument for staying is not complicated. This is the place where she grew up, the place where she married, raised her children and worked beside her husband. As long as she is able to remain there, she wants to.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A 19-year-old was taking a Boston train for the first time when his girlfriend fell onto the tracks; he jumped down to save her and died after hitting the electrified third rail
articles.summary: US News: A 19-year-old man on his first trip on Boston’s public transit system died after jumping onto the tracks to save his girlfriend at Forest Hills statio.
articles.body: A 19-year-old man on his first trip on Boston’s public transit system died after jumping onto the tracks to save his girlfriend at Forest Hills station. Frankey Wright Jr, of Lowell, Massachusetts, died on Saturday afternoon after landing on the high-voltage third rail while trying to pull his girlfriend back onto the platform. His 19-year-old girlfriend was seriously injured in the fall and was taken to a local hospital, where she remains in critical condition. Reports from WHDH 7News and Boston 25 News said the tragedy happened shortly after 1:00 pm on the Orange Line platform in the Jamaica Plain neighbourhood.Sudden loss of balance on the platformAccording to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) Transit Police, the couple had arrived at the station to travel to the annual Caribbean Festival at nearby Franklin Park. Police said the young woman became unsteady near the yellow safety strip, lost her balance and fell from the platform into the tracks. Wright Jr jumped down to help her get back up, but he lost his footing and came into contact with the exposed third rail, which carries 600 volts of direct current. Emergency workers pronounced him dead at the scene. A spokesperson for the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office said transit police are conducting a full investigation, although investigators do not suspect foul play.Tributes to a creative and selfless youthSpeaking to Boston 25 News, the victim’s father, Frankey Wright Sr, described his son as a kind and intelligent young man who worked with children with autism and had created his own clothing line. “My son was a noble young man, and he lost his life trying to save the life of his girlfriend,” Frankey Wright Sr told Boston 25 News. “I'm going to miss my baby.” His sister, Paige Wright, spoke to 7NEWS about the family’s grief and her brother’s instinct to protect others. “I would never think I would lose my youngest brother this early,” Paige said to 7NEWS. “They were excited to go to the festival together. They were going to have a good day.” Paige said her brother’s decision to risk his life showed the kind of person he was, adding: “He loved his girlfriend, and so this really just shows the person that he was. Always trying to help someone and be there for someone.”Calls for stronger safety measures on transit platformsThe incident has led to calls for better physical safety measures across the MBTA subway system to prevent people from falling onto active tracks. In a statement, MBTA Transit Police Superintendent Richard Sullivan expressed sympathy for the family, calling the incident a “horrific tragedy” and offering condolences on behalf of the entire transit agency. However, the victim’s relatives said physical barriers should have been installed to help prevent such accidents. “This was just so unfortunate and just honestly, it shouldn't happen to anybody else. There should have been something there to save him,” Paige Wright told Boston 25 News. The tragedy came as the MBTA was beginning early planning to test platform screen doors, which are protective glass barriers that stay closed until a train stops completely. As reported by Streetsblog Massachusetts, agency spokesperson Joe Pesaturo said the MBTA is preparing a formal request for proposals for a pilot project to study the use of such barriers at selected Orange or Red Line stations.Similar platform safety systems are used on major transport networks across Europe and Asia, as well as at some stations in New York City. They help keep passengers away from moving trains and high-voltage rails. Commuters at Forest Hills station also raised safety concerns when speaking to Boston 25 News. One passenger said protective fencing or automatic gates could help protect vulnerable riders, noting: “Put safety measures in place to kind of make sure that people can't just fall off. It could've been a kid; it could've been anybody.” The Wright family has set up a GoFundMe fundraising page to help pay for funeral expenses for the 19-year-old designer. Meanwhile, local officials continue to examine the safety conditions surrounding the station platform.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Bank of America vice president identified as victim in Times Square attack
articles.summary: Erin Piacenti identified as one of two victims in daytime stabbing on New York City thoroughfare.
articles.body:
A Bank of America vice president has been identified as a victim in a stabbing in Times Square.

Erin Piacenti died from her wounds after the afternoon attack on Monday in the New York City pedestrian thoroughfare, according to the Reuters news agency. Bloomberg News first reported Piacenti’s identity on Tuesday.

Authorities had previously said a female attacker stabbed a 32-year-old woman and a 68-year-old man on West 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue about 4:30pm (20:30 GMT) on Monday. Police fatally shot the suspect at the scene.

The man was in a stable condition in hospital.

“We are shocked and deeply saddened by the ⁠tragic loss of our colleague,” Bank of America said in a statement to Reuters.

“She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed. Our hearts go out to her family ‌and all of her loved ones.”

New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the attack appeared random and unprovoked.

She said responding officers opened fire after trying to Taser the attacker but failed to stop ‌her from advancing towards them with knives.

The attack came weeks after Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty to federal charges connected to the killing of another corporate executive on a New York street. That shooting in December 2024 killed UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and occurred on West 54th Street near Sixth Avenue in Midtown Manhattan.

Speaking in federal court, Mangione admitted to intentionally targeting Thompson as he pleaded guilty to interstate stalking resulting in death.

He faces separate state charges related to the killing although that trial has been postponed in the wake of the federal guilty plea.

Called the “Crossroads of the World”, Times Square sees from 200,000 to 250,000 pedestrians transit through it a day, according to its official website.

articles.title: Summer wildfire call-outs in Lincolnshire more than double
articles.summary: Lincolnshire Fire and Rescue Service says it is proving a "relentless" period for its firefighters.
articles.body:
The number of Lincolnshire wildfires this summer is more than double the amount reported during the same period in 2025, a fire service says.

Lincolnshire Fire and Rescue said it attended 58 during June, July and August, up from 26 the previous year.

The service said they were part of 2,700 incidents, which included false alarm, fire and special service, between 1 June and 25 August, up from 2,022 in 2025.

Chief fire officer Mark Baxter said: "It has been fairly relentless in regards to the amount of incidents our firefighters have attended."

The service is reliant on on-call crews, with the majority of members having another job away from the service.

While Baxter said the amount of incidents appeared to be settling down, he added crews were still "quite busy" across the county.

Speaking on BBC Radio Lincolnshire , he said: "Unprecedented is probably the right word really for June, July and August.

"It's been really demanding for them over the summer period."

The summer has been the hottest on record , according to provisional data from the Met Office.

Fires across England and Wales prompted a government alert in August, warning people not to light anything that could spark a wildfire.

The fire service said it had "not seen a busier summer", with a significant number of fires placing increased demand on firefighters and emergency response resources.

Crews were called out to 58 incidents in Market Rasen in July alone, and Binbrook crews attended six call-outs within a 24-hour period.

"It's just two examples of dozens across the county, with each on-call station showing incredible levels of determination and commitment in serving their communities," the service added.

Baxter explained that for the majority of firefighters, the service was not their primary employment.

"At a moment's notice, they just have to drop everything and respond to their local fire station.

"A huge amount of thanks and recognition needs to go to the businesses and the organisations that release our on-call firefighters and our self-employed personnel, who have to change their working arrangements," Baxter said.

The fire service said the figures for the period could still increase further, with dozens of incidents still being processed and categorised.

articles.title: Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack
articles.summary: A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at the airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes on 4 August.
articles.body:
Germany has said Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig's airport.

A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, on 4 August.

It failed to explode as the detonator was apparently faulty, and investigators suspect a second drone collided with a cargo aircraft nearby. A third drone was reportedly found near the airport 10 days later.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the Leipzig airport attack followed the "well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe" and the assumption was that Germany would be targeted again.

He said the that examination of the equipment used along with intelligence findings proved Russian involvement in the attack.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who was standing beside Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin, said he would order the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, and the contract for the Russian House in Berlin will also be terminated - which many observers have said has been used for espionage and to spread Russian propaganda.

He also announced tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and vowed to increase pressure on Moscow's shadow fleet - old tankers used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Wadephul said he had summoned the Russia's ambassador to Germany, Sergei Nechayev. He was seen arriving at the foreign ministry shortly after the announcement.

The Russian foreign minister said it would respond to "anti-Russian decisions", Interfax news agency reported. Security experts had speculated that Russia may have been responsible, however Russia has always rejected claims of involvement.

Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany is used by the Germany military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carries most of the country's aerial cargo.

The head of Nato, Mark Rutte, said the organisation "stands in full solidarity with Germany".

"The evidence is clear. And I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response," he wrote on X.

The issue was due to be discussed at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland later on Tuesday.

EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression. We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security."

She added that the EU was preparing additional sanctions against Russia.

Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail."

Germany is one of several Nato member states to have reported drone sightings at airports, military and industrial sites over the last year.

Berlin has until now been tight-lipped about who may have been behind the Leipzig attack, except to say the "foreign powers" may have been involved.

US media had already reported that American officials had linked the incident to Russia.

Berlin has warned that the country is the "daily target" of hybrid warfare, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned last week that those who carried out hostile acts against Germany would "pay a price".

The government is looking to boost the powers of its intelligence services, which have long been criticised as relatively toothless, to counter such threats.

Germany is a key backer of Ukraine with Merz forthright in his support for Kyiv.

It is not hard to imagine why Ukrainian cargo planes at a key German logistics hub might be in Moscow's sights.

But this announcement comes at a delicate moment for Merz's government.

A key state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could propel the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) into power at a state-level for the very first time.

The AfD, which is Germany's biggest opposition party, wants to stop sending support to Ukraine and re-open ties with Russia.

In a separate development, German police say they are investigating the discovery of improvised explosive and incendiary devices at a power substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday.

A power line was damage which caused a temporary outage. It is not known who planted the devices.

articles.title: JD Vance calls Michigan Senate candidate El-Sayed 'evil' at campaign rally
articles.summary: El-Sayed faces Trump ally Mike Rogers in what has quickly become a senate race characterised by personal attacks and insults between the two.
articles.body:
US Vice-President JD Vance has described Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as "a very, very evil" person at a campaign rally in Michigan, accusing him of being a divisive figure.

He also warned El-Sayed to "keep my wife's name the hell out of your mouth", after the candidate appeared to suggest that Vance's late grandfather would not accept Second Lady Usha Vance, who is Hindu.

El-Sayed shot back at Vance later on Monday, accusing the Trump administration of pushing "evil" policies and "starting wars abroad when there's peace".

The 41-year-old candidate is facing Trump ally Mike Rogers in what has quickly become a senate race characterised by personal attacks and insults between the two.

Speaking at a rally for Rogers in a Detroit suburb on Monday night, Vance repeatedly accused El-Sayed - who is Muslim - of being a divisive figure with little interest in bringing communities together.

"I realise that there's something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today," Vance said, adding that he was seeking to "destroy" the country.

"My message to Abdul El-Sayed is: You can pal around with terrorist sympathisers, and you can say that America deserved 9/11, or you could empathise not with the children who were targeted at Temple Israel, but with the attacker," the vice-president said.

During his primary, El-Sayed campaigned alongside controversial far-left influencer and Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who once suggested that the US "deserved" the attacks in New York and Washington.

While El-Sayed never said those words and has since distanced himself from Piker, Vance repeatedly linked the two together during his speech.

In an interview with CNN later on Monday, El-Sayed took his own jabs at Vance, accusing the vice-president of a series of "evil" policies during the Trump administration.

"Evil is ripping healthcare away from working people in exchange for tax breaks for billionaires," El-Sayed said. "Evil is making people pay more for groceries and gas while pushing for trade wars and actual war. Evil is dividing people for your own gain. Evil is selling out your morals for a little bit of power."

He also sought to clarify his previous comments about the Vance family and the Second Lady, saying that he was seeking to demonstrate that Vance "believes in a political philosophy that says that some people are somehow more American than others".

The Michigan Senate race is among the most high profile of the upcoming midterm elections and takes place in a key battleground state that former President Joe Biden won in 2020 and Donald Trump won in 2024.

A survey released earlier this week by Michigan firm Epic-MRA suggests Al-Sayed has a narrow four-point lead over Rogers, a former law enforcement officer with long experience in politics.

articles.title: Germany blames Russia for last month's attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
articles.summary: The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced...
articles.body:
BERLIN (AP) — The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives , and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures against Moscow.

The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on the evening of Aug. 4 and the device was defused. German officials said at the time that the incident posed a new level of danger.

Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption across Europe with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Tuesday that authorities found elements such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonator that are "known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine." He said that the device pointed to "a high degree of technical expertise" and painstaking planning, but that the execution of the plan appears to have been left to "low-level" agents.

Dobrindt told reporters in Berlin that intelligence points to "people being involved who acted on behalf of Russian state entities," though he didn't specify which ones. "Taken together, the police investigations, the pattern and intelligence findings prove a Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig airport."

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that "with the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership decided deliberately to do significant damage again to our already massively burdened bilateral relationship." He said that the Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed effective Sept. 18 and the contract under which the Russian House cultural center in Berlin is operated will be rescinded.

Germany will propose the addition of more people from Russia to European Union sanctions lists "in the context of hybrid attacks," will step up entry controls for people from Russia and "increase pressure on the shadow fleet," a reference to tankers suspected of shipping Russian oil in violation of international sanctions. The EU has sanctioned hundreds of "shadow fleet" ships.

Russia's Foreign Ministry told the Interfax news agency that Moscow "would respond" to what it described as Germany's "anti-Russian decision."

Leipzig/Halle is a major hub for international freight and for providing support to Ukraine. The planes that regularly use it include Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.

It is also home to NATO's Strategic Airlift International Solution, or SALIS, which is currently operational almost every day in delivering equipment to NATO battle groups along its eastern flank from Finland to Romania and supporting EU and alliance nation missions.

In 2024, an incendiary device ignited at a logistics center at the airport and set fire to a freight container before it could be loaded onto a cargo plane, part of a plot that Western security officials suspect was organized by Russian intelligence.

articles.title: US borrowing costs hit fresh highs over inflation fears
articles.summary: The effective interest rate on 10 years rose to 4.79%, its highest level since January 2025, as oil prices surged.
articles.body:
US borrowing costs hit a fresh high on Tuesday as renewed strikes in the Middle East pushed up oil prices and heightened concerns over inflation.

The effective interest rate on borrowing over 10 years rose to 4.79%, its highest level since January 2025, as oil prices surged above $92 a barrel.

Such movements on global bond markets affect rates at which the US government can borrow money at, but also influence rates people pay for mortgages, car loans and credit cards.

The spike in borrowing costs comes and fears over the pace of price rises in the US has led to increased speculation that the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates later this month.

Michael Barr, a governor at the US central bank, said in a speech on Tuesday that inflation had been too high for five years and warned if it did not cool "then I think we should act decisively to raise rates".

His comments came after Kevin Warsh, chairman of the Fed, said last week that policymakers would "have work to do" if they were not confident cost-of-living pressures were easing for Americans.

Latest figures show prices rose 3.4% in the year to July, above the Fed's 2% target, however, interest rates have been left unchanged for months between 3.5% and 3.75%.

Warsh has remained tight-lipped about the potential path of interest rates, but investors have been monitoring comments in recent days and expectations of a rate hike this month have grown.

Inflation is concerning both the Fed and global investors, which is driving the increased rates - or yields as they are known - on bond markets.

Governments sell bonds - essentially an IOU - to raise money for spending, and in return they pay interest.

Bond investors typically demand higher returns - or yields - if inflation is high or they expect it to be elevated in the future, and such rates tend to set the path for borrowing costs in economies around the world.

Besides inflation, investors also have concerns about the amount of borrowing from governments around the world as well spending by Big Tech firms, with uncertainty remaining over the return on investment of artificial intelligence.

In the US, national debt has passed the $40tn mark, doubling in just the space of a decade under both the Donald Trump and Joe Biden administrations.

After borrowing costs over 30 years hit levels not seen since 2007, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the the US government would buy back more debt in a bid to lower rates, but the market's reaction to the announcement proved short lived.

In the US 30-year mortgage rates have risen to a one-year high of almost 6.7% following spikes in bond markets.

Rising rates can make borrowing and spending less attractive, which risks dampening economic growth if consumers cut back and businesses halt investment.

articles.title: FRANK SILLER: 'I love you, brother' -- the 9/11 loss that inspired a mission of service
articles.summary: Tunnel to Towers CEO Frank Siller recounts the devastating 9/11 phone call from Richie Obermeyer at Ground Zero that confirmed his brother Stephen would not come home.
articles.body: PROGRAMMING ALERT: Watch Tunnel to Towers Chairman and CEO Frank Siller discuss his new book "Let Us Do Good," on "The Five" on Sept. 1 on Fox News Channel at 5 p.m. ET. There are moments in life that divide everything into before and after. For me, one of those moments came on September 11, 2001, when a firefighter calling from Ground Zero told me what I already feared but was not ready to hear: my younger brother Stephen was not coming home. In that instant, my family’s life changed forever, and so did the course of mine. Even though I knew that it was probably an exercise in futility, I also kept trying to call Stephen from my Nextel phone, on September 11, hoping that perhaps he had somehow already made it over the Verrazzano Bridge and back to Staten Island. We had the same phone; it was both a cellular phone and a walkie-talkie, which was popular in the early 2000s. I kept pressing the button on the walkie-talkie part while I called out for Stephen. He did not pick up. I called again, and again, and again. There was no answer—only an eerie silence. I wound up doing that all night and well into the next few days. I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES Once I got home to join Pat, early in the afternoon, family members began to straggle one by one through my front door. All we could do was sit in my living room and watch the news, just as hundreds of millions of our fellow Americans did that day. I felt like I was dreaming. It was all so surreal, especially since much of the carnage had occurred in my beloved New York City. While it was tempting to excuse myself to go shed a few tears, I understood the need to be strong. I had already deep down accepted the harsh reality of Stephen’s fate and needed to be ready for the moment when other members of my family would soon be sadly forced to do the same—or maybe some already had. AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS That was when my home phone rang. I snuck off into the kitchen to quietly take the call, as not to alarm any family members. On the other end of the line was a neighborhood firefighter named Richie Obermeyer, who lived a few houses away from Stephen. He was calling from the area that would soon be known to America and the world as Ground Zero. Unbeknownst to me, my daughter Elizabeth was watching me take Richie’s call from the hallway. Years later, she gave me her perspective of this exact moment. That’s the thing about tragedy—everyone has their own recollection and personal memory of the way things unfolded. "Hi Frank, it’s Richie Obermeyer. I’m down here at the Twin Towers . . ." he said. "Rich, I’m so sorry. That must be terrible," I said. "It’s just so hard to watch." "Frank, it’s really bad," said Richie. "I’m watching it—" I began to say. "No, Frank." He hesitated and sighed. "It’s really bad." Speaking slowly yet firmly, I tried to tell Richie that I understood while also hoping that he would have the courage to tell me the truth instead of making me ask him point-blank. That’s when Richie finally said it. 9/11 STEEL BEAM ARRIVES AT FLORIDA SCHOOL WHERE BUSH LEARNED AMERICA WAS UNDER ATTACK "No one is coming home, Frank," Richie whispered. "No one." "No one is coming home, Frank," Richie whispered. "No one." I could hardly breathe. My chest started to tighten, and my eyes welled up. I then dropped my head, and tears began rolling down my cheeks. I already knew deep down that my brother was gone, but hearing the news from someone I trusted ushered in a whole new wave of emotion. AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET After I hung up the phone and took a deep breath, I walked into the living room to explain what Richie had told me. Elizabeth jumped into Pat’s arms. My sister Regina let out a startling shriek and yelled, "Not Stephen!" We all felt the same way. How could this have happened to Stephen, our little brother who went through so much in life at such a young age? Not Stephen. Not Stephen, the resilient little boy who became an orphan at the age of ten. His five children—Katherine, Olivia, Genevieve, Jake, and baby Stephen—would now have to live their lives without their father, who was a most spectacular human. Stephen’s wife, Sally, the love of his life, would have to raise these children on her own, perhaps never filling the void Stephen’s death would leave in her heart and soul. How would she do it, emotionally, physically, and financially? It all seemed so impossible. BENJAMIN HALL TACKLES GRUELING ONE WORLD TRADE CENTER CLIMB ON PROSTHETIC LEGS TO HONOR FALLEN HEROES Moments later, we began hugging each other while the tears continued to fall from our eyes. It was truly gut-wrenching. We pulled ourselves together, said a prayer while we were on our knees. One by one, we stood up, bundled into our cars, and drove over to Sally’s house to be together as one family and pledge our everlasting love and support for Sally and the children. Stephen’s life and heroic death serve as a reminder to us all to live life to the fullest and to spend our time here on earth doing good—this is his legacy. When the sun came up on the morning of Tuesday, September 11, 2001, I couldn’t wait to get out onto the golf course with George, Russell, and Stephen. Like I said, the four Siller brothers didn’t get to do this often anymore. As the sun went down on that unimaginably painful Tuesday evening, I repeated the last words I said to Stephen less than twenty-four hours before he became one of the nearly three thousand innocent people killed in the worst terrorist attack in American history. "I love you, brother," I whispered. "See you tomorrow." He had already finished his shift. When he turned his car around to return to his firehouse, FDNY firefighter Stephen Gerard Siller sacrificed his tomorrows so countless others could have their todays. When I later found out the full details of his ultimate sacrifice, it only enhanced my admiration and awe of what Stephen and his fellow first responders so bravely did on that awful morning. Our parents, Mae and George Siller, were devout Catholics and members of the Secular Franciscan Order. We grew up under the guiding philosophy of Saint Francis of Assisi, who famously wrote that "while we have time, let us do good." They were words that all of us lived by, but especially Stephen, as evidenced by his last moments on earth. Stephen’s life and heroic death serve as a reminder to us all to live life to the fullest and to spend our time here on earth doing good—this is his legacy. "A single sunbeam is enough to drive away many shadows," is a quote often attributed to Saint Francis that illustrates how I feel about Stephen’s impact. In the shadows of the collapsed Twin Towers, the memory of my fallen brother helped guide me and all the siblings toward that light. Starting on September 12 and continuing every day thereafter, Stephen’s mission to do good would be my family’s mission as well. God willing, a few others would be willing to help along the way. I never could have imagined just how many kind and generous souls would end up joining the cause. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION To honor Stephen’s memory and the sacrifice of so many that day, my family started the Tunnel to Towers Foundation to carry forward the way he lived his life: by doing good and helping others. His sacrifice became our mission, and today T2T continues that work in service of America’s heroes and their families. articles.title: Spaces in male prisons in England and Wales fall to lowest level of year, sources say
articles.summary: Jails in England and Wales are nearing maximum capacity as the justice secretary prepares to give more details in the Commons on the early-release scheme to free inmates.
articles.body:
The number of available spaces across the male prison estate in England and Wales has fallen to its lowest this year, sources have told the BBC.

As of 1 September, there were about 1,500 free spaces, just under half the number available at the start of June, which Ministry of Justice (MoJ) figures put at 3,040.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris is due to give more details in the Commons later on changes to the early-release scheme, which aims to free up space in prisons as they near maximum capacity.

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced changes to the scheme, which will mean more prisoners, including those convicted of manslaughter, will remain behind bars for longer.

Laundry rooms to be turned into cells to tackle prison overcrowding

MoJ figures show the number of available male prison spaces has been steadily falling since the middle of June, with the last official figures released on 24 August placing them at 1,665.

This week's numbers have not been officially released due to Monday's bank holiday but prison sources say vacancies have fallen once again.

The government has said it would create more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.

An investment of £110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the MoJ said.

The justice secretary told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.

Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly.

"This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."

Norris said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

But the chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."

Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity.

Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being let out of prison in tranches from October.

On Sunday, the prime minister told BBC Breakfast anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.

Extra prison space would also be created by deporting more foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.

Government figures show there were 10,134 foreign nationals held in custody on 30 June, 3,283 of whom were on remand and would not be eligible for deportation.

In the year to June, 5,962 foreign offenders were sent back to their home countries - the highest rate of deportations since 2017 and a 12% increase on the previous year.

articles.title: Locals torch migrant shelters as Spain's PM points blame beyond the border
articles.summary: Ceuta residents burned migrant shelters as Pedro Sánchez accused Russian and Israeli-linked networks of spreading disinformation that fueled the crisis.
articles.body: Residents in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta tore down and burned makeshift migrant shelters amid escalating tensions over a massive influx from neighboring Morocco, as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez accused Russian and Israeli-linked networks of helping spread disinformation that fueled the crisis. Demonstrators carrying Spanish flags moved toward beachside migrant camps last week, destroying shelters and setting fires as police attempted to keep protesters and migrants apart, according to Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE and news agency EFE. Protesters chanted "Invasores, expulsión" — "Invaders, expulsion" — as they advanced toward the beaches where migrants have been staying, EFE reported Aug. 27. Hundreds of residents returned to the streets the following day, marching toward the Trampolín and Benítez beach areas where migrants were camped and repeating the same chant, according to EFE. The unrest follows an unprecedented surge on July 30 and 31, when more than 72,000 migrants irregularly crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, one of the European Union’s two land borders with Africa. At least 100 people died attempting the crossing, according to Ceuta authorities cited by Reuters on Aug. 31. Roughly 5,000 migrants remained in the enclave as of Monday. STATE DEPARTMENT RAISES TRAVEL WARNING FOR PART OF SPAIN AS MIGRANT SURGE SPARKS MILITARY DEPLOYMENT Sánchez on Monday directly linked the mass crossing to what he described as a foreign-backed disinformation campaign. Spanish authorities have said misleading videos and posts circulating on Instagram, TikTok and other social-media platforms falsely suggested that migrants who reached Ceuta by sea would be permitted to remain in Spain. CEUTA MIGRANT SURGE EXPOSES SPAIN-MOROCCO TENSIONS AS ISLAMIST GROUPS REPORTEDLY SEEK TO EXPLOIT BORDER CRISIS Sánchez told radio station SER that research by the European Union’s diplomatic service, the European External Action Service, indicated Russian and Israeli networks had participated in spreading the disinformation alongside far-right networks, Reuters reported Aug. 31. He argued that Russia and Israel had seized on the crisis to attack Madrid because of disagreements with his government over the wars in Ukraine and Gaza. However, Sánchez provided no further details about the evidence supporting the accusation, according to the reports. Both governments rejected his claims. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar accused Sánchez of "lying shamelessly" and said in a post on X that the Spanish leader was attempting to divert attention from domestic policy failures. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov separately rejected Spain’s accusation that Russia was connected to the Ceuta migration crisis. Sánchez also rejected allegations that Morocco’s government deliberately facilitated the border surge, telling SER, "When people talk and speculate about the participation of Moroccan authorities, I deny this outright," according to Reuters. Spanish opposition parties and some human-rights organizations have accused Rabat of allowing the crossings, an allegation Morocco denies. SPANISH JOURNALIST SAYS CEUTA RESIDENTS BELIEVE GOVERNMENT ISN'T DOING ENOUGH TO PREVENT ANOTHER MIGRANT RUSH The disinformation surrounding the Ceuta crossing had been building well before Sánchez publicly accused Russian and Israeli-linked networks. Fox News Digital reported Aug. 4 that an open-source investigation by Golden Owl Intelligence traced weeks of activity across TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp that circulated misleading interpretations of Spanish immigration law, along with information about routes, meeting points and recommended crossing times. The campaign intensified after Spain’s Supreme Court issued a July 8 ruling restricting the immediate return of migrants intercepted at sea near Ceuta and Melilla. Simplified accounts of the ruling, combined with confusion over Spain’s separate plan to regularize hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants, were circulated online as evidence that migrants reaching Spanish territory would be allowed to stay. SPAIN'S MIGRANT SURGE REIGNITES DEBATE OVER EUROPE’S ISLAMIST TERROR THREAT Zineb Riboua, a research fellow at the Hudson Institute, said at the time that Islamist movements were also seeking to exploit the crisis politically. Riboua argued that Islamist voices in Morocco and Spain were amplifying the unrest and portraying Europe as an attractive destination while using Morocco’s ties with Israel and the U.S. to attack the Moroccan government. In a July 31 analysis, Riboua wrote that Islamist activists had spent years encouraging young Moroccans to believe their country offered them little future and depicting Europe as a place where prosperity and opportunity were easily available. The crisis has also spread beyond Spain. Italy on Monday extended for another 15 days its suspension of Schengen free-movement arrangements with Spain, a step first imposed July 31 in response to the mass influx into Ceuta. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Nile Gardiner, director of the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at the Heritage Foundation, warned Fox News Digital at the outset of the crisis that Ceuta could become "a key turning point in the unraveling of the European Union." "Once you unravel Schengen — which I think is inevitable — this breaks down the entire European project," Gardiner said. Reuters contributed to this story.

articles.title: 80,000-year-old stone points in Uzbekistan resemble weapons used in France 25,000 years later, raising questions about how humans reached Europe
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At the Obi-Rakhmat rock shelter in northeastern Uzbekistan, researchers have identified tiny triangular stone points in the site's oldest occupation l.
articles.body: At the Obi-Rakhmat rock shelter in northeastern Uzbekistan, researchers have identified tiny triangular stone points in the site's oldest occupation layers, dating to around 80,000 years ago. The unretouched micropoints average less than 2 centimetres in width and weigh only a few grams, with their dimensions indicating that they were designed for very small, lightweight projectile systems. The researchers argue that their shape and fracture patterns are consistent with use as projectile heads on arrow-like shafts. What makes the discovery particularly striking is that virtually identical micropoints appear at Mandrin Cave in France's Rhône Valley roughly 25,000 years later, where they are associated with an early presence of Homo sapiens in western Europe. The two groups of points are separated by about 6,000 kilometres, yet share an unusually similar form and evidence of projectile use. The researchers do not claim that one directly descended from the other, but say the resemblance raises important questions about how lightweight projectile technology emerged and spread across Eurasia.How researchers identified the tiny weapons hidden in an 80,000-year-old rock shelterObi-Rakhmat was discovered in 1962 and lies at an elevation of about 1,250 metres in the western foothills of the Tian Shan Mountains in northeastern Uzbekistan. Excavations have exposed roughly 10 metres of Pleistocene deposits spanning around 40,000 years, preserving a long sequence of human activity. For the new study titled Arrow heads at Obi-Rakhmat (Uzbekistan) 80 ka ago?, researchers examined material from the site's deepest layers, particularly layers 20 and 21, which date to around 80,000 years ago. Rather than assuming that every pointed stone was a weapon, the team conducted a preliminary traceological investigation designed to distinguish projectile damage from fractures created during stone-tool production or other activities. From the material studied, the researchers selected 20 pieces that could be regarded as projectile armatures on the basis of their morphology and impact damage. They identified three broad classes: relatively massive points, tiny micropoints and bladelets. The micropoints were particularly significant because some showed fracture patterns and microscopic linear impact traces consistent with use as projectile heads. The authors stress that this is still a preliminary study based on material from only about 20 square metres of excavation, but say the sample is sufficient to demonstrate the presence of impacted micropoints in the oldest layers.Why the size of the Obi-Rakhmat points matters so muchThe most unusual pieces are the triangular micropoints. Unlike the site's larger projectile points, they are extremely small and lightweight: the fractured specimens in the study have an average weight of 1.4 grams, ranging from 0.7 to 2.5 grams, while their average width is 18.2 millimetres. Their dimensions are important because the researchers argue that the points are too narrow to have functioned effectively as tips for larger projectile weapons. Geometric calculations indicate a potential shaft diameter of roughly 7.5 to 8 millimetres, which falls within the dimensions expected for an arrow shaft. The researchers therefore consider arrow-like shafts the most straightforward interpretation, while acknowledging that another technical possibility has not been experimentally tested. The evidence becomes more significant because the micropoints occur alongside much larger projectile points and bladelets. The almost complete large points weigh around 25 to 35 grams, making them substantially heavier than the micropoints. The researchers therefore suggest that the assemblage represents several types of hunting weapons rather than a single standardised projectile system. They also note that the production of the micropoints appears to have responded to a specific need for small, lightweight sharp armatures, although the precise way every bladelet was used remains uncertain.What connects Uzbekistan's tiny points to arrows found in France 25,000 years laterThe most striking comparison comes from Mandrin Cave in the Rhône Valley of France. A layer at the site known as layer E, dating to approximately 54,000 years ago, contains tiny projectile points that the Obi-Rakhmat researchers describe as effectively identical to the Central Asian micropoints. Those French points were also impacted by use as projectile heads and have been interpreted as arrowheads. The same layer contained a deciduous tooth belonging to Homo sapiens, while a later Mousterian layer at Mandrin contained Neanderthal remains. The Mandrin occupation is therefore considered evidence for an early pioneering presence of modern humans in southern Europe. The two assemblages are separated by roughly 25,000 years and about 6,000 kilometres, yet the researchers were struck by how closely their micropoints resemble one another. However, they explicitly stop short of claiming that Obi-Rakhmat and Mandrin represent a direct technological lineage. Instead, they say the similarity raises the possibility that comparable technological solutions could have spread between different human groups or been developed independently. Similar combinations of larger points, micropoints, blades and bladelets are also beginning to be identified at other Middle Palaeolithic sites in Europe, including Cueva Millán in Spain and Riparo l'Oscurusciuto in Italy.Why scientists are cautious about saying Homo sapiens made the Uzbekistan arrowheadsThe discovery does not establish that Homo sapiens were living at Obi-Rakhmat 80,000 years ago, and the researchers are careful to separate the technological evidence from the question of biological identity. The site's human remains are limited, and its population history remains debated. Instead, the researchers make a technological argument: projectile points occasionally found at Neanderthal sites tend to be larger and do not clearly form a separate class of lightweight projectile armatures, whereas the combination of different projectile types, including microlithic points apparently designed specifically for lightweight weapons, has so far been documented at sites associated with modern humans. Even so, the authors do not identify the Obi-Rakhmat hunters as Homo sapiens. Their comparison with Mandrin is therefore significant without proving a migration route. If future excavations reveal more of these tiny projectile points at sites between Central Asia and western Europe, they could help determine whether the technology represents a shared tradition that moved between populations, repeated independent inventions or a technological solution that emerged in several regions under similar hunting pressures. For now, the discovery provides evidence that sophisticated lightweight projectile technology existed in Central Asia around 80,000 years ago, thousands of years before the similar technology documented at Mandrin.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
