articles.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: River water smashed into tunnel and chased me, hydropower engineer says
articles.summary: Major efforts to rescue hydropower workers continue as Nepal's death toll exceeds 1,000.
articles.body:
Nepalese hydropower workers have told the BBC about the catastrophic moment water from the Trishuli River crashed into their tunnel as the region was inundated by deadly flash floods last week.

It started with a sudden, strong gust of air, says Pemba Dundu Tamang, whose team of about 30 was constructing the tunnel's concrete lining.

The blast of wind sent plywood flying through the air and dislodged heavy machinery. Just outside, houses had already been swept away.

"I ran towards the tunnel entrance," he said. "The water was chasing behind me and I was running ahead of it."

Tamang lost several family members who were at home at the time. Nepal's death toll has exceeded 1,000 after last week's devastating floods, and officials say about 4,000 are missing.

A number of the missing - potentially in the hundreds - are labourers like Tamang, working in a vast network of tunnels at hydropower sites along the river. Engineers have been pumping air into these tunnels as part of a huge rescue operation.

"We are focused on search-and-rescue efforts at the tunnels, our work is continuing," Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP news agency.

"Our soldiers are also deployed to collect bodies and prevent the spread of disease."

Tamang says he ran for about 20 minutes to flee the violent deluge, which followed him uphill.

"I was almost unconscious with shock. I could not think clearly."

His colleague, Itha Ghale, says the powerful gust of air almost blew them away as they sprinted.

Over 99% of the electricity generated in Nepal comes from hydropower, and Tamang and Ghale had been working at a major production site helping to build the Upper Trishuli 3B Hydropower Project.

The plant, which was due to open next year, was designed to re-use water from a hydroelectric plant further upstream to generate additional electricity for Nepal's national grid.

There were several different teams operating there - and Tamang says the one operating the large tunnel-lining machine was the last to come out.

But soon afterwards came a crushing realisation.

"I could see where my house should have been. There was nothing left. That was when I realised everything was gone."

Six of Tamang's relatives - his mother, elder brother and sister-in-law and three of their children - are gone, he said. They were at home on the riverside when the floods hit.

Only his wife, son and one nephew survived.

"I feel life is meaningless now. Surviving feels miserable. I do not know where to eat or where to go," Tamang says.

"The dead are at peace. It is those of us who survived who suffer."

Ghale, who lost eight members of his family, says he does not know why he survived. "Perhaps it was not my fate to die."

The eight family members include his mother and eldest daughter. His three sons and wife survived.

Tamang dreads what the future may bring, especially if these hydropower projects are shut down. "If things continue like this, we will go hungry. Sometimes I feel it would have been better not to survive."

Tamang ultimately managed to take refuge with a few others in the village of Shanti Bazar for two days until the army came to rescue them.

He estimates about 50 to 60 workers were able to escape the tunnel alongside him.

He says more people could have been saved if proper resources had been in place.

This is echoed by a new report which says there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the disaster - and that better early warning systems could have saved lives.

Satellite images suggest the glacier surface was moving faster, meltwater was turning brown and a crack was developing in the surrounding rock, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment.

These are all possible signs the mountainside was becoming unstable.

The avalanche itself moved too fast for conventional warnings to help those closest to it, the scientists say.

But further downstream, where the flood took 10 minutes or more to arrive, they say a comprehensive warning system could potentially have saved a significant number of lives.

Right now, however, specialists from China, India and Nepal are continuing to use excavators and heavy machinery to blast through debris from the hydropower projects to try to reach workers still trapped at several hydropower sites.

"There are probably still some survivors inside. I would be happy if they were rescued quickly," Tamang says.

"I know many people who are still trapped there."

articles.title: Reform's Richard Tice says UK must adapt to changing climate
articles.summary: Richard Tice said he will not "resile" from his comments on people enjoying the hot weather.
articles.body:
The UK should "learn to adapt to the changing climate, rather than arrogantly think you can stop the power of the sun", Reform UK's deputy leader has said.

According to the Met Office, this summer is the hottest on record, with five separate heatwaves.

Ahead of the party's national conference in Birmingham this week, Richard Tice was asked about climate change, including criticism he received for previously telling people they should enjoy the prolonged hot weather.

"I get criticised all the time, but it's true isn't it? People have enjoyed the warm weather," he told BBC South East.

"I'm 61. I remember 1976, half a century ago, it was a similar summer day," Tice added.

The 1976 heatwave saw a drought declared as temperatures peaked at 35.9C in Gloucestershire.

Fifty years on and the UK is fresh from a summer that saw 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F), eclipsing the previous record of 34 days.

Clear that he will not "resile" from his comments that the hot weather improves the quality of English wine, Tice argued that climate change is nothing new.

"The climate has always changed for millions of years, it always will," he said.

The world's climate has changed naturally throughout history, but natural causes cannot explain the particularly rapid warming seen over the last century, according to the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

In addition, the world's 11 warmest years on record have all happened since 2015, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

Tice added: "I think we should celebrate our successes such as the English wine and sparkling wine industry."

The deputy leader believes that the UK's efforts in this space have been unrewarded.

Tice said: "We've done more than our bit; we've halved our Co2 emissions in the last 30 years. Globally, Co2 emissions continue to soar."

According to the Office for National Statistics, an estimated 367 million tonnes of carbon dioxide were emitted by the UK last year - a 54% reduction since 1990.

Tice further claimed that UK energy prices have "doubled in seven years because of net zero and the cost of renewals" but this has made "no difference to global Co2 emissions".

Last week, it emerged that energy prices for millions of households will rise to the highest level for three years because the Iran war has resulted in higher wholesale gas prices.

Last month, BBC Verify cited the cost of wholesale gas as one of three reasons why bills have soared.

Another is that the UK generates a relatively high share of its electricity from natural gas, while billpayers are also helping to fund the building of electricity grid infrastructure.

According to industry body Energy UK, the typical household's dual-fuel bill is now 70% higher than it was at the start of 2021.

articles.title: Red state heartlands put a ring on young love while progressive blue cities lag on early marriage
articles.summary: IFS research reveals young adults in their twenties marry at far higher rates in middle America than in New York or Los Angeles metro areas.
articles.body: Young people looking to tie the knot in their twenties may want to rethink where they live. Moving to big coastal cities like New York and Los Angeles could mean lowering the odds of getting married— and living in an area with a high concentration of singles may not lead to more marriages. According to a new study from the Institute for Family Studies (IFS), early-marriage rates are lower in many urban hubs and higher in parts of the heartland. The findings point to a geographical divide in family formation, with young adults in places like Tennessee, Indiana and Utah marrying at higher rates than their coastal big-city peers. "For singles, your best odds of finding love and getting married aren’t in big coastal cities where most singles live, but in middle America, where more marriage‑minded singles are," Wendy Wang, senior researcher at the Institute for Family Studies, told Fox News Digital. THE STATES REVEALED AS BEST TO START A FAMILY AMID CRATERING BELIEF IN THE AMERICAN DREAM The research is part of the IFS’s "Get Married Maps," which provides young people with information about regional marriage trends and examines factors associated with marriage rates. Those factors include employment, religion and recent presidential election results, among others. "Given the many benefits of marriage, a city where more young people are tying the knot might ultimately provide a more fulfilling life than one with just excellent entertainment and tasty food—but few weddings," the study explains. For adults ages 22-29, regions with the highest marriage rates include Provo, Utah, as well as parts of Tennessee, Indiana, Nebraska, Kentucky, Idaho, North Carolina, Kansas and Georgia. In contrast, eight of the ten regions with the lowest early-marriage rates are concentrated in the New York and Los Angeles metropolitan areas. NORTH TEXAS DOMINATES IN POPULATION GROWTH AS BIG BLUE CITIES FAIL TO RECOVER TO PRE-PANDEMIC LEVELS "These findings demonstrate that, for young adults, the ‘best place’ to get married may depend largely on when they hope to marry. Those who are committed to marrying in their twenties may want to think carefully about moving to a major coastal city; meanwhile, those same cities could be an excellent option—though not the only choice—for marriage-minded adults in their thirties," the study notes. While coastal cities have lower marriage rates for 20-somethings, the picture changes for singles in their thirties. For adults ages 30 to 39, regions with the highest marriage rates include portions of the New York, San Jose, Los Angeles and Chicago metropolitan areas, along with suburbs in Texas and Indiana. POLL FINDS SHARP RISE IN YOUNG MEN CALLING RELIGION 'VERY IMPORTANT' Wang also explained that the research shows living in an area with a large population of single young people may not improve the odds of finding a future spouse. "If you think your best chance of finding someone to marry is in the places with the most singles, think again," Wang told Fox News Digital. "The nation’s top 10 areas with the highest share of singles (more than 80 percent unmarried) are far from the places where most new marriages are happening." The IFS research found that areas with more single men relative to single women tend to have higher female marriage rates, but the relationship is even stronger when researchers measure the ratio of full-time-employed single men to all single women. Military-adjacent regions like Oceanside, California, and Fayetteville, North Carolina, as well as tech-heavy areas such as Mountain View and Sunnyvale, California, have some of the highest ratios of full-time-employed single men to single women. DRIVEN BY PROGRESSIVE DOOMISM, LIBERALS ARE HAVING FEWER BABIES THAN CONSERVATIVE FAMILIES However, the link between male income and marriage rates varies by age. For women in their thirties, regions with a higher ratio of single men earning at least $60,000 a year had higher marriage rates. That financial link disappears for women in their twenties, suggesting younger couples place less emphasis on high salaries when deciding to tie the knot. Still, on an individual level, young men in their twenties who earn $60,000 or more are about twice as likely to marry as lower earners. "Single men’s jobs remain one of the strongest factors driving marriage in America," Wang added. Regional marriage rates for young adults in their twenties also showed a strong positive correlation with areas that backed Donald Trump over Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. However, for adults in their thirties, this correlation flips and turns negative. "One possible explanation is that more rural parts of the country, where Trump generally performed better than Harris, often have higher marriage rates for adults in their twenties," the study notes. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The researchers noted that their findings show broad regional patterns, not proof that a particular location or political environment causes people to marry. The study measures where respondents currently live, not necessarily where they met their spouses or lived when they got married. The researchers also acknowledged that some people may have moved after marrying, potentially affecting the marriage rates of certain regions.

articles.title: A Staten Island deli manager started paying kids for better report cards 3 years ago; his fundraiser has now crossed $500,000 and he is giving school supplies to 3,000 students
articles.summary: US News: A Staten Island deli manager who started giving neighbourhood children cash and free snacks for getting top marks three years ago has turned his small.
articles.body: A Staten Island deli manager who started giving neighbourhood children cash and free snacks for getting top marks three years ago has turned his small reward programme into a major community effort, raising more than $500,000 (£380,000) to provide school supplies to 3,000 students. Wail “Wally” Alselwi, who manages the express deli on Staten Island and is known locally as "Island Ock", first became widely known online after sharing videos in which he gave students cash and let them choose anything they wanted from his store in return for straight-A report cards. Reporting by ABC News and Good Morning America shows how Alselwi’s viral school reward programme grew into a major fundraising campaign. It eventually led to a large back-to-school giveaway for thousands of local children before the new school year.Academic rewards that sparked a movementAlselwi started the programme after noticing that many young people in the neighbourhood needed more motivation and encouragement for their schoolwork. He began giving cash from his own pocket, along with free drinks, crisps and household groceries, to children who showed him strong report cards. The programme quickly grew after a video filmed inside his shop showed 12-year-old customer Zameir Davis celebrating an excellent report card. The video went viral on TikTok. In the clip, Alselwi told the student he could take anything he wanted from the shelves. The gesture received widespread praise and encouraged many other local children to bring their grades to the deli. In an interview with ABC News broadcast on Good Morning America, host Danny New explained how Alselwi’s personal gesture soon attracted support from people around the world. Social media followers offered money to help him reach more children. Over three years, donations to Alselwi’s GoFundMe campaign continued to grow, taking the total raised beyond $500,000.Supplying thousands of students for the new school termWith strong financial support from social media followers and people in the community, Alselwi expanded the programme from rewarding individual children at the deli to organising a large educational giveaway. Before the new school term, Alselwi arranged for fully stocked backpacks to be bought and prepared for 3,000 students across Staten Island. The bags included stationery, notebooks, pens and other essential classroom supplies. According to coverage from the Staten Island Advance (SILive.com), the fundraising campaign passed $550,000. This allowed Alselwi to expand the giveaway to include both primary and secondary school students in districts where families need the most help. During an appearance on ABC News, Alselwi spoke about how quickly the project had grown and the effect it has had on young people working hard at school. "It started with just one kid coming in with a good report card, and now seeing thousands of kids motivated to do well in school is incredible," Alselwi said during his interview with Good Morning America. "We want every child to feel supported and ready on their first day of class."Community support and long-term expansion plansLocal parents and community leaders have praised Alselwi for creating a simple reward system that encourages children to work hard at school while also helping families with the cost of buying supplies for the new academic year. According to NBC News, local residents often gather outside the Staten Island deli at the end of each school term. Children line up along the street, carrying their report cards to show Alselwi. Alselwi has also said he plans to continue his report card reward programme at the deli throughout the school year. Money left from the online fundraising campaign will continue to support cash rewards, educational materials and food incentives for students who achieve strong grades or show clear improvement in their schoolwork in the months ahead.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Alps murders: Luger in a lake gives hope for French cold case
articles.summary: Saad al-Hilli was shot dead with his wife and mother-in-law while holidaying in eastern France in September 2012.
articles.body:
Police investigating the unsolved murder of a British family in France 14 years ago have an unexpected new clue with the discovery of a Luger pistol in the waters of a nearby lake.

One of the few certainties in the killings of Saad al-Hilli with his wife and mother-in-law – as well as a passing cyclist – is that they were shot through the head with a Luger model P06, a type used by the Swiss army until around 1960.

Now France's cold case unit has confirmed the discovery of a Luger in Lake Annecy, not far from the scene of the murders in September 2012.

According to Marianne magazine, which broke the story, it was British tourists on 20 August who found the weapon lying in two metres of water.

At first they thought it was a water pistol, but realised their mistake when they felt its weight.

The discovery was made near the very camping site – Le Solitaire du Lac – where the al-Hillis were staying in their caravan, Marianne reported.

Forensic experts are now examining the weapon, which has been badly damaged by its time under water, to see if it is indeed a P06 model.

It is estimated that around 60,000 Luger P06s were manufactured. But the number of Luger pistols in general that were made is more like three million.

Exhaustive investigations in France and the UK have left police no closer to understanding who carried out the al-Hilli murders and why. Over the years a series of leads have been pursued then dropped.

A British national of Iraqi birth, Saad al-Hilli was holidaying with his family in the picturesque countryside of Lake Annecy in eastern France.

On the afternoon of 5 September, his body with those of his wife and mother-in-law were found in their car, its motor still running, on a forest road near the village of Chevaline. A passing cyclist had – like the other victims – been shot through the head.

Poignantly, the two al-Hilli daughters, aged four and seven, survived. The older girl had been hit on the head with a pistol butt and was badly hurt. The younger, lying in the car under her mother's skirts, was not discovered till forensic experts began examining the scene many hours later.

It was fragments from the pistol butt which enabled police to identify it as a Luger P06. The model is regarded more as a collector's item than a working weapon, which made the theory of a professional hit against the family seem less likely.

Lake Annecy is only 50km from Switzerland, where the Luger P06 will have been familiar to older people from their military service. French police said many examples of the gun have been kept by families on either side of the border.

Among the theories that have been entertained are that the murders were linked to a family row over money; that they were the work of a motiveless crank; and that the main target was the cyclist.

Police were also briefly intrigued by the fact that al-Hilli's wife's first husband – an American – died of a heart attack just hours before the killings in France.
